‘학교’ (school) + the location particle ‘에서’ (at/in).
‘-이’ marks ‘학생’ as the subject of the sentence (used after a consonant).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The student is in the classroom.

definitions.note: short form of 하나; commonly used before a noun in counting (native Korean numbers)
Past adnominal (modifier) form of 하다; used to describe a noun (e.g. ‘the thing (someone) did’).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: This is the homework I did.

definitions.note: “한국말” means the Korean language; “-을” is the object particle.
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 저는 한국말을 조금 할 수 있어요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I can speak a little Korean.

definitions.note: Object form of 한국어 used with the particle 를.
Plain style present form of 하다, used in writing and in formal or instructional contexts (can sound blunt in conversation).
Plain (informal) present tense form of 하다; often used in writing, narration, or informal speech.
Often used to mean 'formerly' or 'in the past,' sometimes with a nuance of 'for a while' depending on context.
Often used to mean “(just) try” or “let’s do it (once)” in suggestions/requests (e.g., 해 봐요 = try doing it).
Used to emphasize that doing something even a single time would be enough (often with requests, suggestions, or in negative sentences).
This is the topic form of 한자 (“as for hanja / Chinese characters…”).
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 한자는 한국어 어휘를 이해하는 데 도움이 돼요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Hanja (Chinese characters) help you understand Korean vocabulary.

definitions.note: Used before a noun to mean “to do” / “that will be done” (e.g., 할 일 = “things to do”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I have a lot of things to do today.

definitions.note: This is the modifying form of 하다, used before a noun to mean “to do” / “that (someone) will do.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I have a lot of things to do.

definitions.note: 할아버지 + topic particle 는 (“as for grandpa…”)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Grandpa takes a walk in the park.

definitions.note: Often used with ~와/과 or ~랑/이랑 to mean "together with."
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I went to the movie theater together with a friend.

definitions.note: formal polite style (합니다체) present tense statement form of 하다
polite, formal present tense of 하다; commonly used in formal speech and writing

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I always drink coffee in the morning.

definitions.note: informal (해체); used as the conjugated form of 하다
Informal (해체) present form of 하다; used with friends, family, or someone younger.
Used with the subject marker -가.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The year has changed (A new year has begun).

definitions.native: even if (someone) does, even though (someone) does
definitions.note: From 하다 + -아/어도; used to mean “even if/though” or “it’s okay to do.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: It’s okay even if you do it now.

definitions.native: try it, give it a try
definitions.note: informal command; often used to encourage someone to try doing something
Connective form of 하다 used to link reasons or sequences (roughly “because (I) do …” / “do … and then …”).
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 비가 와서 집에 있어서 심심해서 책을 읽었어요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: It rained, so I stayed home, and I was bored, so I read a book.

definitions.note: Used to express necessity/obligation (하다 + -아/어야). Often followed by 해/해요/합니다 (e.g., 해야 해요 = “have to do”).
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 오늘은 일찍 자야 해서 숙제를 해야 해요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I have to do my homework because I need to go to bed early today.

definitions.note: polite informal (해요체) form of 하다; commonly used as a light verb after nouns (e.g., 공부해요 = study)
present tense, polite (해요체) form of 하다; also commonly used as a generic ‘to do’ verb in many expressions

definitions.native: do it for me, do it for us
definitions.note: informal/polite request form of 해주다; often used when asking someone to do something for you
Past tense of 하다 with the clause ending -는데, often used to give background or set up a contrast before the next clause.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I did the homework, but it was 너무 hard.

definitions.note: Past form of 하다. Often used as an auxiliary after patterns like -기도 to mean something like “(even) did / did (sometimes)” for emphasis or added nuance.
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 나는 가끔 혼자 영화관에 가기도 했다.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I sometimes even went to the movie theater alone.

definitions.note: past tense of 하다 (“to do”); also commonly used to make many nouns into verbs (e.g., 숙제했다 “did homework”).
Past attributive (modifier) form of 하다, used before a noun to mean “that (someone) did.”
informal past form of 하다; used in casual speech
informal/polite past tense of 하다, used in casual speech (to someone close or younger)
Past tense of 하다 (“to do”), in the polite informal style (해요체).
attributive form of 행복하다; used before a noun (e.g., 행복한 사람 “a happy person”)
“형제” usually refers to brothers or male siblings; in some contexts it can mean “siblings” in general. “-가” is the subject marker.

definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 저는 오늘 집에서 혼자서 영화 봤어요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I watched a movie at home alone today.

definitions.note: Attributive form of 혼자이다 used before a noun (e.g., ‘an alone person’).
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 혼자인 사람은 조용히 책을 읽고 있었어요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The person who was alone was quietly reading a book.

definitions.note: This is the noun 화 (“anger”) with the subject marker -가 attached.

definitions.native: to the bathroom, in the bathroom
definitions.note: The particle 에 marks a destination/location (to/at/in).
Formal polite expression used to greet someone (e.g., to welcome guests, visitors, or new members).
“효과가” is “효과” + the subject marker “가” (meaning “an effect/result” as the subject of the sentence).
used after a noun to mean “after (something)”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I met a friend after class.

definitions.note: Attributive form of 훌륭하다, used before a noun.
Used to emphasize a big difference, often in comparisons (e.g., 훨씬 더 = “much more”).
This is 흡연 (smoking) + 은, a topic marker meaning “as for smoking / smoking is…”.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Smoking is bad for your health.

definitions.note: attributive form of 흥미롭다; used to describe a noun (e.g., “an interesting book”)
describes something (or someone’s situation) that is difficult; attributive form of 힘들다 used before a noun
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: These days it’s a very difficult time at work.
